summary.text: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation with whole-number coefficients where only whole-number answers count.
The name honours Diophantus of Alexandria, a Hellenistic mathematician of the 3rd century who studied such equations.
Hilbert's tenth problem shows that no general method can decide whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation has a whole-number solution.

facts.label: Linear kind
facts.value: A sum of unknowns with coefficients equals a constant

facts.label: Exponential kind
facts.value: Unknowns are allowed to appear in exponents

facts.label: General theories
facts.value: Beyond linear and quadratic cases, a twentieth-century achievement

facts.label: Famous hard case
facts.value: Fermat's Last Theorem took over three centuries to solve

items.prompt: Which question is the kind that a Diophantine equation is built to answer?

options.label: How many whole boxes of two sizes add up to exactly 50 items?
What is the exact height of a ladder leaning on a wall?
What is the average of a long list of test scores?
How fast is a falling stone moving after two seconds?

items.explain: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation with integer coefficients where only integer solutions are of interest, and you cannot buy half a box.

items.prompt: A programmer claims to have one program that takes any Diophantine equation and always says whether a whole-number solution exists. What is wrong with the claim?

options.label: The program would run correctly but take too long
It only works if the equation has a single unknown
No general method of this kind can exist at all
It would need the equation to be linear and nothing else

items.explain: Hilbert's tenth problem shows that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation has an integer solution.

items.prompt: A student wonders why these equations carry such an odd-sounding name. What is the explanation?

options.label: They honour David Hilbert, who first posed them as a problem
They were named after Pierre de Fermat, who wrote about them
The name comes from a Greek word meaning whole numbers
They honour Diophantus of Alexandria, who studied them long ago

items.explain: The word refers to the Hellenistic mathematician Diophantus of Alexandria, who studied such equations in the 3rd century.

items.prompt: An equation has an unknown number sitting in the power spot, like some number raised to the power x. Which name fits that type?

options.label: Linear Diophantine equation
Exponential Diophantine equation
Quadratic Diophantine equation
Homogeneous Diophantine equation

items.explain: An exponential Diophantine equation is one in which unknowns can appear in exponents, whereas a linear one just sums unknowns with coefficients.

items.prompt: A friend says, 'These are just puzzles from school algebra, so mathematicians surely had a full theory of them centuries ago.' What is the better picture?

options.label: Individual equations are old puzzles, but general theories beyond linear and quadratic cases came in the twentieth century
General theories were complete in the 3rd century, and only individual puzzles came later
No general theory of any kind exists, even for the linear and quadratic cases
General theories arrived at the same time as Diophantus and have not changed since

items.explain: Single equations have been treated as puzzles throughout history, but general theories beyond the linear and quadratic cases are a twentieth-century achievement.

items.prompt: Methods exist that work on almost every cubic equation met in practice. What does that tell us about solving every cubic Diophantine equation?

options.label: Cubic equations are known to be easier than quadratic ones
A complete method exists but has not been published
Every cubic equation can be settled by the same short recipe
No algorithm is known that works for every cubic equation

items.explain: For degree three there are general methods that work on almost all equations met in practice, but no algorithm is known that works for every cubic equation.
